Hebrews 1.audience: Hebrews does not name its author or its readers. Its readers knew the Greek Old Testament well, had suffered for their faith (Hebrews 10:32–34), and are greeted by "they of Italy" (Hebrews 13:24). Early writers suggested Paul, Barnabas, Luke, or Apollos as author.

culture.title: A chain of Scripture
culture.text: The chapter quotes seven Old Testament passages, from Psalms 2, 45, 97, 102, 104, and 110 and 2 Samuel 7:14.

culture.title: Angels and the law
culture.text: Jewish tradition held that angels were present when the law was given at Sinai (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19).

culture.title: The right hand
culture.text: Sitting at a king's right hand was the place of highest honor and authority (Psalm 110:1).

Hebrews 2.audience: The writer and readers received the message from those who heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3), so they were not first-generation eyewitnesses.

culture.title: Drifting
culture.text: "Let them slip" translates a word used for a ship drifting past its harbor.

culture.title: Captain
culture.text: The word means a leader or pioneer who goes first and opens the way.

culture.title: Fear of death
culture.text: Philosophers such as Epicurus wrote to free people from the fear of death.

Hebrews 3.audience: The writer compares Jesus with Moses and quotes Psalm 95 about Israel's rebellion in the wilderness.

culture.title: Faithful in all his house
culture.text: God calls Moses "faithful in all mine house" in Numbers 12:7.

culture.title: To day
culture.text: Psalm 95 was sung in synagogue worship. It recalls Israel at Massah and Meribah (Exodus 17:7).

Hebrews 4.audience: The writer continues from Psalm 95, urging readers to enter God's rest.

culture.title: God's rest
culture.text: The writer quotes Genesis 2:2 about God resting on the seventh day.

culture.title: Jesus and Joshua
culture.text: "Jesus" here is the Greek form of the name Joshua, the leader who brought Israel into Canaan.

culture.title: A two-edged sword
culture.text: The Greek word for "discerner" gives us the word ‘critic.’

Hebrews 5.audience: The writer explains Jesus as high priest after the order of Melchisedec (Psalm 110:4) and rebukes the readers for being "dull of hearing" (Hebrews 5:11).

culture.title: Taken from among men
culture.text: Under the law the high priest was chosen from Aaron's descendants (Exodus 28:1).

culture.title: Milk and strong meat
culture.text: Greek teachers commonly called basic lessons ‘milk’ for beginners.

Hebrews 6.audience: The writer warns against falling away and assures the readers of God's oath to Abraham (Genesis 22:16–17).

culture.title: The ground that bears thorns
culture.text: Farmers burned fields overgrown with thorns and thistles.

culture.title: Oaths
culture.text: An oath ended a dispute; people swore by someone greater than themselves.

culture.title: An anchor
culture.text: The anchor was a common symbol of hope and safety, and was later carved in early Christian catacombs.

Hebrews 7.audience: The writer discusses Melchisedec from Genesis 14:18–20 and Psalm 110:4.

culture.title: Without genealogy
culture.text: Priests had to prove their descent from Aaron by genealogy (Ezra 2:61–62). Genesis gives no genealogy for Melchisedec.

culture.title: Tithes
culture.text: Levites received tithes from the other tribes (Numbers 18:21).

culture.title: Judah and the priesthood
culture.text: Jesus was from the tribe of Judah, not Levi.

Hebrews 8.audience: The writer quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 on the new covenant, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament.

culture.title: Pattern shewed in the mount
culture.text: Moses built the tabernacle according to the pattern shown him on Sinai (Exodus 25:40).

culture.title: Ready to vanish away
culture.text: Hebrews speaks of priests still offering gifts (Hebrews 8:4), which some take as a sign it was written before the temple's destruction in AD 70.

Hebrews 9.audience: The writer describes the tabernacle, its furniture, and the high priest's yearly entry into the most holy place on the Day of Atonement.

culture.title: The tabernacle furniture
culture.text: The candlestick, table, shewbread, golden censer, and ark of the covenant with the pot of manna, Aaron's rod, and the tables of the covenant (Exodus 25; Numbers 17:10).

culture.title: Once every year
culture.text: Only on the Day of Atonement did the high priest enter behind the veil with blood (Leviticus 16).

culture.title: A testament
culture.text: The same Greek word means both ‘covenant’ and ‘will,’ and a will takes effect only after death.

Hebrews 10.audience: The writer recalls the readers' early sufferings: public insults, imprisonment of some, and the seizure of their goods (Hebrews 10:32–34).

culture.title: Sacrifices every year
culture.text: The sacrifices of the Day of Atonement were repeated every year.

culture.title: A gazingstock
culture.text: The word was used for being exposed to public ridicule, as in a theater.

culture.title: Spoiling of your goods
culture.text: When Claudius expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, property could be seized or abandoned.

Hebrews 11.audience: The writer lists people of faith from Abel to the prophets, drawing on the Old Testament and later Jewish history.

culture.title: Sawn asunder
culture.text: A Jewish tradition, recorded in The Ascension of Isaiah, says that Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

culture.title: Tortured, not accepting deliverance
culture.text: 2 Maccabees 7 tells of a mother and seven sons tortured under Antiochus IV who refused to give up the law, hoping in the resurrection.

culture.title: Sheepskins and goatskins
culture.text: Prophets like Elijah wore rough garments (2 Kings 1:8). During the Maccabean revolt the faithful hid in mountains and caves (1 Maccabees 2:28).

Hebrews 12.audience: The writer urges readers to run with endurance and contrasts Mount Sinai with "mount Sion" (Hebrews 12:18–24).

culture.title: A cloud of witnesses
culture.text: Spectators filled the stadium at athletic games. Runners stripped off anything that would weigh them down.

culture.title: Chastening
culture.text: The writer quotes Proverbs 3:11–12. Fathers had full authority to discipline their children.

culture.title: Esau's birthright
culture.text: Esau sold his birthright for a meal of pottage (Genesis 25:29–34).

Hebrews 13.audience: The letter closes with practical commands, news that Timothy has been released, and greetings from "they of Italy" (Hebrews 13:23–24).

culture.title: Entertaining strangers
culture.text: Abraham welcomed three visitors who turned out to be messengers from God (Genesis 18:1–8).

culture.title: Remember them that are in bonds
culture.text: Prisoners relied on friends and family for food and care.

culture.title: Without the camp
culture.text: Bodies of sin-offering animals were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem's walls (John 19:17, 20).

James 1.audience: James writes "to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad" (James 1:1). Tradition identifies him as James the brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church, whom Josephus says was stoned around AD 62.

culture.title: Scattered abroad
culture.text: The Diaspora (‘scattering’) was the name for Jews living outside the land of Israel.

culture.title: The flower of the grass
culture.text: Spring flowers wither quickly under the hot east wind. James echoes Isaiah 40:6–8.

culture.title: Looking in a glass
culture.text: Mirrors were polished bronze and gave a poor reflection.

James 2.audience: James warns against favoring the rich in the assembly and argues from Abraham and Rahab that faith is shown by works.

culture.title: Gold rings and goodly apparel
culture.text: Gold rings were worn by the equestrian class, the wealthy order just below senators in Rome.

culture.title: Your assembly
culture.text: The Greek word is synagoge, the usual word for a Jewish meeting.

culture.title: The devils also believe
culture.text: "God is one" recalls the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), recited daily by devout Jews.

James 3.audience: James warns teachers about the power of the tongue, using images from daily life.

culture.title: Bits and helms
culture.text: Greek moral writers often used the horse's bit and the ship's rudder as examples of small things controlling large ones.

culture.title: The course of nature
culture.text: The phrase literally means ‘the wheel of birth,’ a phrase also used in Greek religious writings.

culture.title: Fountains, figs, and olives
culture.text: Springs in the Jordan valley and around the Dead Sea could be fresh or brackish.

James 4.audience: James addresses quarrels among believers and merchants who make plans without God.

culture.title: Traders
culture.text: Merchants traveled between cities for a year or more at a time to buy and sell.

culture.title: A vapour
culture.text: Morning mist disappears quickly as the sun rises.

James 5.audience: James condemns rich landowners who withhold wages and urges patience, pointing to the prophets, Job, and Elijah (James 5:10–17).

culture.title: Wages kept back
culture.text: The law required day laborers to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14–15).

culture.title: The early and latter rain
culture.text: In Israel the early rains came in October–November and the latter rains in March–April (Deuteronomy 11:14).

culture.title: Anointing with oil
culture.text: Olive oil was a common treatment for illness and wounds (Luke 10:34; Mark 6:13).
